idiom_name: assert()/abort() for broken invariants + immediate error-code return at the first failed check
implementation_notes: C has no exceptions, so fail-fast is two hand-written mechanisms. For a broken internal invariant, assert() prints the failing expression with __FILE__ and __LINE__ and calls abort(); for a request that cannot be served, the function returns its error value at the first check and every caller has to propagate it immediately - each call site is a hand-maintained guard, and a wrapper macro or warn_unused_result is what keeps it from being forgotten. Because abort() does not run atexit() handlers and leaves open resources to the implementation's choice, cleanup stays the caller's job; the classic form is the only form, and it is justified exactly where a library must not terminate its host process (use a distinct error return there) or where an invariant breach makes continuing undefined.
pitfalls: assert() expands to nothing when NDEBUG is defined, so it can never guard input or capacity in a release build - production behaviour would differ from the test behaviour.
abort() skips atexit() handlers and closes open streams only as the implementation chooses, so resources acquired before the failing assertion can leak; POSIX only guarantees the SIGABRT handling.
Error codes are easy to drop: without a propagation convention (wrapper macro, warn_unused_result) a caller continues after a failed check, which is exactly the fail-slow failure mode.
